q: Ultimately the outcome was great but there were many points in labour where a lack of information about my own physical progress and baby's wellbeing meant that I could not make informed choices and do not want other women to go through the same experience.
cx: After a three-day labour ending in an emergency caesarean, she says she lacked information to make choices.
r: medical: emergency c-section, fetal distress context

q: trust your instincts and do not feel pressured to stick to your birth plan in changing circumstances.
cx: One of her lessons from a long UK labour: drop the birth plan when circumstances change.

q: Apparently I will be waiting 7-10 days for the bile acid test to return. I'm terrified, feel alone and anxious, and I'm so scared for my baby.
cx: At 33 weeks, waiting over a week for a test result after new symptoms, she feels alone and scared.
r: medical condition named; fear for baby

q: I was struggling with my mom telling me she “knows me” and knew that I wouldn’t be able to do it.
cx: Early in pregnancy her mother told her she would not manage the unmedicated home birth she planned.

q: I got a lot of responses telling me that I was severely underestimating childbirth, that I should listen to my mom, and that I was too young (24) to think rationally about it. Eventually, I deleted the post because the comments really got to me.
cx: Strangers online told her she was too young and naive about birth; she deleted her post.

q: I wasn’t completely prepared for how painful birth would actually be, but i didn't try to be. I knew it would be the worst pain I'd have ever felt and was okay with that.
cx: Eleven weeks postpartum, on how she approached the pain of an unmedicated birth.

q: Looking back, I’m glad I didn’t let those comments change my mind. I listened to myself, prepared as much as I could, and trusted that I would handle whatever happened.
cx: She had the birth she planned, in the Netherlands, and is glad she ignored the doubters.

q: The hardest part for me was being extremely tired towards the end. So my biggest advice is: sleep as much as you can in the weeks leading up to your due date!
cx: After a 45-hour labour with little sleep, exhaustion was the hardest part.

q: My husband and midwife were both amazing! There wasn’t actually much they could do, and I was in my own little world most of the time, but they stayed calm and supportive throughout. My husband held me for pretty much my entire labor.
cx: Her husband and midwife's calm support during a home birth.

q: I just bought a maternity kit (Kraampakket) which is a box containing medical supplies like sterile gauze, cord rings, and mattress protectors. It was like 30 euros. I also bought new linens.
cx: In the Netherlands, where insurance covers birth, her only home-birth purchase was a 30-euro maternity kit.

q: Lastly my husband just shaming girls saying how much he don’t want a girl it’s too much for him he want a son that’s it, if it’s a girl we won’t be having anymore kids because he doesn’t want the risk of having another girl.
cx: First-time pregnant woman upset to learn she's having a girl partly because of her husband's words.

q: So finding out I was having a girl made me feel like I failed my husband and that it was just going to be a miserable experience.
cx: After the sex reveal she felt she had failed her husband.

q: My husband also admits that what he said was wrong and he was just saying things but he’s excited for his girl. He said this is my kid I’ll be proud no matter what. Hearing those things cheered me up.
cx: Her husband took back what he said and told her he would be proud no matter what.

q: I researched myself into a pretty dark hole.
cx: Older first-time mother, after a late-pregnancy scan finding, on what her own online research did.

q: The epidural I thought I could wait for happened so fast. I was scared to death to get one, and honestly I didn’t even notice it was happening bc of the contractions.
cx: During induction the epidural she dreaded came quickly and she barely noticed it.

q: My first baby was born in April 2020, during the height of the uncertainty surrounding the pandemic. It was the week hospitals were still deciding whether spouses would even be allowed in the delivery room, and partners weren’t permitted to stay during recovery.
cx: Mother of three recalls her first birth in 2020 when partners might be barred from the ward.

q: Coming home brought a whole new set of challenges. I worried about the pandemic, struggled with my milk coming in, and tried to navigate being a first-time mom while isolating from others and running on very little sleep with a colicky baby.
cx: Her first weeks home with her first baby: isolation, feeding struggles, little sleep.

q: My second birth was a much better experience, and labor was significantly faster. Things felt like they were looking up, but I still carried so much pressure and guilt when it came to feeding my baby.
cx: Her second birth went better, but guilt over feeding followed her again.

q: Instead of simply feeling exhausted by the constant wake-ups, I find myself appreciating them. I know these newborn days are fleeting, and knowing this is our last baby makes me want to soak in even the smallest moments.
cx: With her third and last baby the newborn wake-ups feel different.

q: I’ve finally made peace with the fact that nursing may not be for me. I no longer feel the same pressure to make it work at all costs.
cx: Third time round she let go of the pressure to breastfeed.

q: Looking back, I wish I had given myself more patience and grace during those first two postpartum experiences. I wish I had understood sooner that motherhood doesn’t have to look perfect to be beautiful
cx: After three babies, what she wishes she had known after the first two.

q: I was shocked. I’d been so convinced it was a boy that I had to take a moment to grieve the child I’d imagined having. And I think it’s important to be honest about that, because those feelings don’t mean you won’t love the child you’re carrying.
cx: At the 20-week scan she learned it was a girl and needed time to adjust.

q: So, if you’re scared about having a daughter, I just want you to know that it’s okay to feel that way.
cx: Mother of a 16-week-old girl reassures pregnant women afraid of having daughters.

q: I’m using this brand called ancient minerals and it says to use the ENTIRE 8 lb BAG and that is psycho, but you do need to use **way more than you think** […] It’s kind of expensive and annoying to do every night but got damn if it didn’t work for me!!
cx: At 38 weeks after weeks of sleeplessness, she found nightly bath salts expensive but worth it.

q: I have been struggling for WEEKS with insomnia - like 5-6 hours of bed flopping per night - I am 38 weeks now
cx: Weeks of sleepless nights at the end of pregnancy.

q: What really bothered me was when the consultant said “if we had caught this earlier, we could’ve monitored it better,” when I had been asking and turned down for extra scans since June.
cx: UK mother repeatedly refused extra scans; later a consultant said earlier detection would have helped.
r: medical: scan findings, emergency c-section; mental health mentioned

q: In every scenario, I wanted to be the one who was wrong. Every mum with anxiety does. I’m glad I pushed through even when they made me feel silly for overreacting.
cx: On pushing for monitoring despite being made to feel she was overreacting.

q: I also don’t remember feeling like I had a care team who continued to really care for me after delivery. It felt like once my baby was out, the focus shifted entirely to her, and I was left behind.
cx: Recalling her first birth: after delivery all attention went to the baby and she felt left behind.
r: medical condition: postpartum complication in first birth

q: I think I spent so much time preparing for the possibility of history repeating itself that I didn’t fully consider the possibility that things could go well, too.
cx: Just after a calmer second birth, on spending the pregnancy braced for a repeat of the first.

q: I was TERRIFIED when I found out I was pregnant for the second time and didn’t think I’d survive it tbh.
cx: Second pregnancy after a frightening first postpartum.
r: medical condition: prior complication; survival fear
